title: Telecom Manufacturing Zone Gwalior: 25 LoIs Explained
summary: Gwalior TMZ, 19 Nov 2026: LoIs to 25 firms, the ₹493 crore lab-led plan, MP incentives checked, telecom PLI compared and the jobs for ECE engineers.
body_markdown:
On 19 November 2026, the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) and the Madhya Pradesh government handed Letters of Intent (LoIs) to 25 companies that plan to set up units in the Telecom Manufacturing Zone (TMZ) in Gwalior. The handover took place at a ceremony in Bhopal, and Phase II of the zone was announced at the same event. PIB's advisory the day before called these "Letters of Intent for land allotment". Phase I covers about 170 acres, given free by the state, and the Centre is funding ₹


493 crore of its infrastructure. The government has not named the 25 companies or said what each will invest.


This post separates what the official releases confirm from what was only reported. It shows where the ₹


493 crore goes and checks Madhya Pradesh's incentive arithmetic against its own rules. It also compares the zone with the telecom PLI scheme and explains how a telecom box is actually built and certified in India. We end with the roles electronics and telecom engineers could target.


## Key facts at a glance


- **19 Nov 2026, Bhopal:** LoIs went to 25 companies investing in TMZ Gwalior, in the presence of Chief Minister Dr Mohan Yadav and Communications Minister Jyotiraditya M. Scindia, and Phase II was announced. Source:[PIB release 2338585](https://pib.gov.in/PressReleasePage.aspx?PRID=2338585) .
- **₹ 493 crore from the Centre** for Phase I. In the budget shown in Madhya Pradesh's investor deck, ₹


270.24 crore (54.8%) goes to testing facilities and the lab ecosystem. Sources: PIB, 30 Jul 2026; MP investor deck hosted on dot.gov.in.
- **About 170 acres** of Phase I land, given free by Madhya Pradesh: 100 acres in the SADA area and 70 acres in the Gwalior IT Park. The zone is run by a special purpose vehicle (SPV) owned 51% by the state and 49% by DoT. Source: PIB, 30 Jul 2026.
- **₹ 5,500 crore in commitments** from the New Delhi and Mumbai investor meets. PIB has tied this to 18,000 jobs (Aug 2026) and "nearly 20,000" (19 Nov 2026). Sources: PIB, 4 Aug and 19 Nov 2026.
- **Reported, not in PIB:** the 25 LoI holders account for about ₹


3,600 crore and 15,600 jobs. A further 450 acres were cleared for six more companies. Source: Free Press Journal, 19 Nov 2026, quoting Scindia.


**Courses:** the hands-on skills a telecom plant needs are covered in Skill-Lync's[5G Testing](https://skill-lync.com/electronics-engineering-courses/5g-test) and[Advanced PCB Design Using Altium](https://skill-lync.com/electrical-engineering-courses/advanced-pcb-design-altium-ecad-software) courses.


## What was announced in Bhopal on 19 November 2026?


DoT and the Madhya Pradesh government held an LoI distribution ceremony in Bhopal for 25 companies investing in TMZ Gwalior, and announced Phase II of the zone. PIB published the release at 5:29 pm on 19 November. The release describes an integrated cluster of about 170 acres for telecom equipment, components, optical fibre, software and passive infrastructure.


PIB had flagged the event a day earlier, on 18 November, as a ceremony for "Letters of Intent for land allotment ... to prospective investors". That wording matters. An LoI is a step before a plant: it tells a company it can have a plot. It is not a factory, a production licence or a disbursed incentive. PIB itself calls the handover a step towards "translating investor interest into manufacturing opportunities on the ground".


At the ceremony, Scindia said India must "move from being a services nation to becoming a product nation". The Chief Minister said the state Cabinet had approved 170 acres of land for the zone. The Madhya Pradesh government also presented the project and its roadmap, but PIB did not publish the roadmap.

## What is a Telecom Manufacturing Zone, and what scheme is behind it?


A Telecom Manufacturing Zone is a dedicated industrial estate for telecom products. Factories, shared test labs and R&D sit side by side on plug-and-play plots, so a company can rent ready buildings rather than build from scratch. Gwalior's is the first. It rests on a 30 July 2026 MoU between DoT and Madhya Pradesh, not on a nationally notified scheme. We found no DoT scheme notification for TMZs in general.


The MoU release and the state's investor deck (which DoT hosts on its website) spell out how the zone works:


- **Who runs it.** An SPV, set up by the state as a private limited company, owned 51% by Madhya Pradesh and 49% by DoT. Its six-member board has three central and three state nominees and is chaired by the DoT Secretary. MPIDC (the state industrial development corporation) is the master developer.
- **Where it is.** Phase I(A) is in the Gwalior IT Park and Phase I(B) is at Kuletha in the SADA (Counter Magnet City) area: 170.5 acres in the deck. The deck puts the site about 8 km from Gwalior railway station, 15 km from the airport and 300 km from Delhi.
- **How the land is used.** 52.1% of the Phase I area is for industry, 18.6% for roads, 9.2% for logistics and the rest for services, open space, housing and shops. That is about 88.8 acres of factory plots.
- **How big it could get.** The MoU release called the TMZ a "350-acre" cluster, with projected investment of ₹


12,000-15,000 crore over time. Later releases describe a 170-acre Phase I. Phase II was announced on 19 November with no official size.


The money from the Centre is ₹


493 crore in grants. The deck's line items show what kind of zone DoT is paying for. More than half of the money is for test labs, not sheds.


The deck's "total indicative outlay" is ₹


493.44 crore. Testing labs and the zone's internal infrastructure take 91.2% of it.


The deck lists two labs. Lab A covers six product domains:


- 5G core network functions (AMF, SMF, UPF and others)
- satellite terminals (VSAT, BUC, LNA/LNB)
- optical fibre cable (duct, buried, ADSS, OPGW)
- SIMs, including eSIM (eUICC)
- passive optical network (PON) gear (OLT, ONT, ONU)
- routers (BNG/BRAS, MPLS)


Lab B is a pair of security-testing labs for 5G and 4G systems, Wi-Fi CPE, IoT devices and PON equipment. The deck marks both Lab B units "Phase-I". A shared test lab inside the zone could spare a small manufacturer from sending every new product elsewhere for testing, if the labs win the accreditations and designations that certification requires.

## What incentives does a company in the zone get?


Madhya Pradesh carries most of the incentive cost. Its package gives a 50% capital subsidy on eligible fixed capital investment (EFCI), capped at ₹


200 crore. Land comes at a ₹


1 premium and ₹


1 per square metre a year for 30 years. A new employee earns the company up to ₹


5,000 a month for five years (for units investing over ₹


75 crore), plus ₹


13,000 of training support. There are freight, power and R&D subsidies too. The state says it will spend nearly ₹


8,000 crore to attract ₹


12,000 crore of investment over 10 years.


The deck backs that up with three worked cases. A ₹


50 crore unit with 170 employees gets ₹


32 crore from the state (64% of project cost). A ₹


100 crore unit with 270 employees gets ₹


75 crore (75%). A ₹


500 crore unit with 1,200 employees gets ₹


350 crore (70%). The deck does not show how it reached those totals, so we rebuilt them from the three rules it itemises:

## How does the TMZ sit next to the telecom PLI scheme?


The two do different jobs. The production-linked incentive (PLI) for telecom and networking products pays a percentage of extra sales, wherever in India the product is made. The TMZ offers a place: free land, ready buildings, shared test labs and state subsidies. The anchor firms named for the zone in July (Dixon, HFCL, Tejas Networks, VVDN and Syrma SGS) all appear among the 42 PLI beneficiaries, Dixon through Dixon Electro Appliances.

A Gwalior plant that starts production in 2027 or later would have to rely on the state package rather than the current PLI. We found no notified successor scheme as of 20 November 2026. None of the TMZ releases say whether a unit can claim both.


## What will factories in the zone make?


The official releases list the target product areas but name no factory and no specific product. The areas are mobile devices, optical fibre, telecom equipment, components, software, passive infrastructure and 5G/6G technologies. The MoU release names routers, antennas, optical fibre and chips as critical items. The PLI covers a similar list, including core transmission equipment, 4G/5G radio access network gear, customer premises equipment (CPE), IoT access devices, and enterprise switches and routers. When the Cabinet approved the scheme in February 2021, PIB put India's telecom equipment imports at more than ₹


50,000 crore.


A fair reading is that the zone's lab list shows what DoT expects to be made nearby: PON boxes, routers, 5G core and radio gear, satellite ground terminals, SIMs and fibre cable. That is our inference from the deck, not a commitment by any company. For background on two of those product lines, see our explainers on[optical fibre types](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/optical-fiber-cable-optical-fiber-types-what-makes-them-unique) and on[chip packaging (OSAT) in India](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/semiconductor-osat-india) .


## How is a telecom product actually built, tested and certified?


Most telecom boxes start as printed circuit boards assembled on a surface-mount technology (SMT) line. Each unit is then tested electrically, built into its enclosure and tested again, including RF tests for radios. Separately, each product model must be certified under DoT's MTCTE regime (and NCCS security testing where it applies) before it can be sold, imported or used in India.


Rows 1 and 2 happen to every unit; row 3 happens once per product model. A simplified view: real lines differ by product.


### 1. Board assembly on the SMT line


A stencil prints solder paste onto the board's pads. Solder paste inspection (SPI) then measures each deposit in 3D. Pick-and-place machines set down the chips, passives and RF parts, and a reflow oven melts the paste into joints. Automated optical inspection (AOI) checks the result with cameras. Parts whose joints are hidden underneath, such as BGAs, need X-ray. Texas Instruments' assembly notes for one of its wireless modules give the same core sequence (print, paste-volume check, placement, reflow) and add X-ray checks before and after reflow for bridging and voids.


### 2. Test and box build


On mixed boards, through-hole parts such as power connectors, terminal blocks and large capacitors go in after reflow and are wave- or selectively soldered. An in-circuit test (ICT, a fixture that probes every net), or a fixtureless flying-probe tester, catches opens, shorts and wrong part values. Boundary scan (JTAG) tests connections that probes cannot reach. The boards then go into the enclosure with fans and RF cables, and a functional test powers the box up and checks that it works as a product. Radios get RF tests for output power, spectrum and calibration. 5G NR base stations are tested to 3GPP TS 38.141-1 for conducted measurements and TS 38.141-2 for radiated (over-the-air) ones.


### 3. Certification before sale


India's Mandatory Testing and Certification of Telecom Equipment (MTCTE) requires telecom equipment to be tested and certified before sale, import or use. A lab designated by the Telecommunication Engineering Centre (TEC) tests each product against its Essential Requirements, and TEC issues the certificate. The procedure was framed in October 2018 and applied to the first network elements from 1 October 2019. Security is tested separately: the National Centre for Communication Security (NCCS) runs the ComSec scheme. Under it, products are tested against Indian Telecom Security Assurance Requirements (ITSARs) at designated security test labs. Lab B in Gwalior is meant to do this kind of testing.


For a hands-on view of the board side, see our[PCB design courses](https://skill-lync.com/courses/pcb-design) . The radio side is covered in[5G NR Radio Access Network](https://skill-lync.com/electronics-engineering-courses/5G-NR-New-Radio) .


## What jobs could the TMZ create for ECE and telecom engineers?


The government's job figures are projections, not hires. The July MoU release projected about 14,000 direct skilled jobs, with about 3,500 in Phase I. Investor-meet totals since then have ranged from 18,000 to "nearly 20,000". Using PIB's own ₹


5,500 crore and 18,000 jobs, that is about ₹


30.6 lakh of investment per job. Nobody has published a hiring timeline.


The lab domains and the process above point to concrete roles. Our earlier overview of[job roles for electronics engineers in telecom](https://skill-lync.com/blogs/trending-job-roles-for-electronics-engineers-in-the-telecom-industry) covers the operator and network side; the list below is the factory side:


- **SMT process and quality engineers:** stencil and reflow profiles, SPI/AOI programmes, yield. These suit ECE and EEE freshers who know PCB assembly and soldering defects.
- **Test engineers (ICT/FCT):** fixtures, test scripts in Python, boundary scan, failure analysis. Our[Telecom Testing (4G) with Python and Robot Framework](https://skill-lync.com/electronics-engineering-courses/telecom-testing-4g) course covers the scripting side.
- **RF test and calibration engineers:** spectrum and signal analysers, conducted versus over-the-air measurement, 3GPP test cases. Start with[Fundamentals of Wireless Communication](https://skill-lync.com/electronics-engineering-courses/fundamentals-wireless-communication-telecom-engineers) .
- **Certification and compliance engineers:** preparing MTCTE and ComSec submissions, reading Essential Requirements and ITSARs, working with test labs.
- **Lab engineers in the shared labs:** 5G core, PON, router and security testing. The labs are DoT-funded, and[5G Core](https://skill-lync.com/electronics-engineering-courses/5G-Core) and[5G Testing](https://skill-lync.com/electronics-engineering-courses/5g-test) skills apply directly to them.
- **Hardware and embedded design:** the "design in India" part the ministers keep stressing (and the reason the PLI pays +1% for design-led products). See our[embedded systems courses](https://skill-lync.com/courses/embedded-systems) .


For pay benchmarks in adjacent roles, see Skill-Lync's[embedded engineer salary page](https://skill-lync.com/salaries/embedded-engineer) . If you are preparing for PSU or core-company routes,[GATE ECE](https://skill-lync.com/gate/electronics) covers the analogue, communications and electromagnetics fundamentals that RF test roles use.


## What is still unknown?


- Which 25 companies got LoIs, what each will make, and what each plans to invest. PIB has given only totals from earlier investor meets.
- When construction and production start. No date appears in any release after the 6 October announcement of a 29 October bhoomipujan.
- Phase II's size and cost. One report says the state Cabinet cleared 450 more acres for six companies, but no official Phase II figure has been published.
- Whether the shared labs will be accredited and designated for MTCTE and ComSec testing. That is what would make them useful to manufacturers.


We will update this post when DoT or Madhya Pradesh publishes the list of LoI holders or a construction schedule.


## Frequently asked questions


### What is the Telecom Manufacturing Zone in Gwalior?


It is an industrial cluster for telecom manufacturing, R&D and testing, set up under a 30 July 2026 MoU between DoT and Madhya Pradesh. Phase I covers about 170 acres in the Gwalior IT Park and the SADA area. It is run by an SPV owned 51% by the state and 49% by DoT, with ₹


493 crore of central funding.


### Which companies got Letters of Intent on 19 November 2026?


PIB says 25 companies received LoIs but has not named them. In July, PIB named Dixon Technologies, HFCL, Tejas Networks, VVDN and Syrma SGS among the anchors of the proposed zone. That does not confirm that any of them is among the 25.


### Is the TMZ the same as the telecom PLI scheme?


No. The PLI pays 4-7% (plus 1% for design-led products) on incremental sales of eligible telecom products made anywhere in India, from a ₹


12,195 crore outlay. The TMZ is a physical zone with free land, ready buildings, shared test labs and Madhya Pradesh's state incentives.


### How many jobs will the Gwalior TMZ create?


Official projections range from about 14,000 direct skilled jobs (July MoU release) to "nearly 20,000" (19 November release). They are based on commitments made at investor meets. No company has announced hiring for a Gwalior plant yet.


### What skills do telecom manufacturing plants hire for?


They hire for SMT process and quality, in-circuit and functional test, RF test and calibration, certification under TEC's MTCTE and NCCS security rules, and hardware and embedded design. Python scripting, RF measurement basics, PCB knowledge and familiarity with 5G and PON standards are the most transferable skills.
